::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[On the use of the "min" function / operator in epsilon-delta limit proofs: how does " delta = min {a,b}" guarantee " delta <a AND delta < b"?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3568328/on-the-use-of-the-min-function-operator-in-epsilon-delta-limit-proofs-how-d), asked by user655689 on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2020-03-03; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Below a limit proof that requires in the end the use of the " min" function. 
>
> I know I have to use " delta = min {a,b} " but I do not understand clearly how the " min function" does the job. 
>
> Can it be shown formally that " *delta = min { 1, epsilon/15}* " guarantees that : 
> "*( delta < 1 AND delta < epsilon /15)".* 
>
> My question : how to explain the step from (8) to (9) in the proof below? 
>
> Also: when checking a delta value in the form of  "*min { a, b}"*, do I have to proceed to a double verification, one for *a*, and one for *b*?
>
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: FcOKy.png
:::

Either $a \leq b$ or $b \leq a$.  The minimum is equal to one and less than the other.  So it's *less than or equal* to both.

If $|x-1| < \delta$, then either:
$$|x - 1 | < \delta = a < b$$
or 
$$|x - 1 | < \delta = b < a$$
Either way, $|x-1| \leq a$ and $|x-1| \leq b$ both hold.
